extracted.intended_audience: Harvard undergraduate mathematics students considering or writing a senior thesis
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative standards for selecting a topic/adviser, conducting meetings, writing an expository (or occasionally research) senior thesis in mathematics, and preparing for the oral examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding an adviser and topic
rubrics_metrics.description: How and when to identify an adviser and a thesis topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested approaches: follow up on an REU topic by looking up relevant faculty; ask faculty members at the end of junior year; take a graduate course with a research component and write a thesis on that; approach professors in an area you're interested in. Practical tips: ask faculty how much time they can spend on you, knock on doors during the spring semester of junior year so you can line up topic/adviser before summer, shop around if someone says no, ask post-docs, fellows, and preceptors, and consider a 'shadow adviser' in the department if your main adviser is outside Math.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisor meetings — frequency and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectations for meeting cadence and what meetings should cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meet once every week or two (some advisers want weekly; different advisers vary). Meetings typically include discussing what you read, presenting a proof on the board, and asking/answering questions. The adviser may ask what you read and what questions you have. Bring a list of unclear points and take notes. Be prepared to work with your adviser's schedule and to adapt to differences in how much time advisers want to see you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis examination expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: What happens at the oral examination and what examiners typically probe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exam is generally oral and should last less than two hours. Examiners may ask for the intuitive meaning of results, ask you to state and prove main result(s), ask you to work out examples of main results, ask leading questions to guide you, and probe side results, connections to other fields, or background material. Prepare by reading through your thesis several times and have examples of main results worked out in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start early and manage time
rubrics_metrics.description: Timing and time-management expectations for thesis work and writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start early—talk to potential advisers in junior spring and try to have topic/adviser lined up before summer so you can read over the fall and begin writing in January or February at the latest. Time spent typically grows exponentially as the submission deadline approaches; many students work heavily over January. Advice from students: start earlier, start writing earlier, share writing earlier with your adviser, and seek feedback sooner. Use the Writing Center earlier rather than late.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dealing with getting stuck
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended strategies to overcome blocks during research/writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include: read different books and more background, try to work out an example, take a break and return later, talk to roommates/friends/grad students, move on to other parts and come back, write an explanatory email to your adviser (even unsent) which can help, and make a list of unclear points to bring to meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and level of exposition (what to include/prove)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deciding how much to write and which lemmas or details to include.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of a clone of yourself before starting and ask what would have been helpful to learn the topic. Part of the process is making decisions about what to leave out. Write so the idea is transmitted clearly; if something is not explanatory, put it in an appendix. You do not necessarily need to prove every lemma—include what a motivated reader needs to understand the topic. Aim to 'teach your topic to someone who doesn't know the subject.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how much original research is expected in the senior thesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The thesis is not supposed to contain original research; it should be an original exposition of material rather than a publishable paper. If original results appear, they will probably be at most one chapter. Some theses that won highest honors were purely expository. The desire to obtain original results should not be the starting point for a thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing an appropriately-sized topic
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on selecting a manageable scope for the thesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students are often too ambitious; focus on a bite-size piece of math and understand it really well. Create the reference you wish you'd had when starting. Advisors may need to re-in in students; choose a manageable topic rather than an overly broad one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisor role and student responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarifies the adviser-student relationship and responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The thesis is the student's project; the faculty is not a co-author and typically will not 'crack the whip.' Students must self-motivate. The faculty's role is to help find readings, send you in interesting directions, help understand the math, and advise on writing. Ask how much time an adviser can spend and request more frequent meetings or feedback if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines for applied theses
rubrics_metrics.description: Special considerations when the thesis has applied or interdisciplinary content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied theses are allowed, but ensure there's a shadow adviser in math if your adviser is outside the department. Explain mathematical methods in detail when using them for applied results. Be careful with technical words from the other discipline—replace them mentally with a placeholder (e.g., 'smurf') to check where you need further explanation; if many 'smurfs' appear, explain more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing writing and requesting feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Best practices for drafting, sharing, and revising thesis writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Share writing earlier with your adviser and after each chapter; ask for more feedback progressively. Use the Writing Center for help on writing (preferably earlier). When pressed for time, writing becomes harder, so start chapters as soon as content is certain. The writing process is an opportunity to make the exposition pedagogical and engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting/exam preparation tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete actions to be ready for meetings and the oral exam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare by reading through your thesis several times before the exam, have worked examples of main results ready, be ready to state and prove main results, and prepare lists of questions/unclear points for meetings. Practice presenting proofs (e.g., on the board) during meetings to simulate examination conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives and benefits of doing a thesis
rubrics_metrics.description: What students are expected to gain from undertaking a senior thesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary goals include learning deeply about a topic, understanding key papers, assessing interest in grad school or a professional math career, getting experience learning independently (no syllabus), and enjoying the one-on-one process with an adviser. Some students pursue a thesis to obtain an honors degree.
